reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / RCOG and FIGO placenta accreta spectrum guidance
clinicalPearls: The spectrum ranges from accreta (villi adherent to myometrium) through increta (invasion into myometrium) to percreta (through the serosa, sometimes into bladder)
The strongest risk factor is a placenta praevia overlying a previous caesarean scar, with risk rising sharply as the number of prior caesareans increases
Other risks include previous uterine surgery, endometrial curettage, and assisted reproduction
Antenatal detection by ultrasound (loss of the clear zone, placental lacunae, bladder-wall interruption) allows planned care and improves outcomes
Magnetic resonance imaging can supplement ultrasound to clarify the depth and topography of invasion, especially posteriorly
The condition threatens catastrophic haemorrhage at delivery because the placenta fails to separate from the uterine wall
Optimal management is planned delivery at a specialist centre, often by scheduled caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ
A multidisciplinary team, blood product availability, and critical care support are essential for safe delivery
reference.pathophysiology: Placenta accreta spectrum results from defective decidualisation, usually over a uterine scar, so that chorionic villi anchor directly to or invade the myometrium rather than the normal decidua basalis. The absent decidual plane prevents physiological placental separation after delivery, and attempts at removal tear deeply vascular tissue, producing torrential haemorrhage. Deeper invasion (increta and percreta) can breach the uterine serosa and involve adjacent structures such as the bladder, with abnormal neovascularisation increasing operative bleeding.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound with colour Doppler
Magnetic resonance imaging to assess depth and posterior or parametrial extension
Assessment of placental location relative to any prior caesarean scar
Cystoscopy or urological assessment when bladder involvement is suspected
Baseline haemoglobin, group and antibody screen with crossmatch
Coagulation profile and planning for major transfusion support
redFlags: Antepartum haemorrhage in a woman with praevia and prior caesarean
Haematuria suggesting bladder invasion in percreta
Signs of concealed or overt major obstetric haemorrhage
Unplanned diagnosis at delivery with a non-separating placenta
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are substantially better with antenatal diagnosis and planned delivery at an experienced centre; unrecognised cases carry a high risk of massive haemorrhage, transfusion, bladder injury, and maternal death. Many women require hysterectomy, with consequent loss of fertility.
pitfalls: Failing to screen women with praevia and a previous caesarean for abnormal invasion
Attempting forcible manual placental removal, precipitating uncontrollable haemorrhage
Delivering in a unit without immediate access to blood products and specialist surgery
Underestimating percreta with bladder involvement and omitting urological input
references: RCOG guidance on placenta praevia and placenta accreta
FIGO placenta accreta spectrum consensus guidelines
